title: Thought Leadership: A Corporate Conversation

jokes.text: Frank asks if the reporter is from a newspaper while the gang panics about dumping 500 gallons of baby oil in the Schuylkill River with 200 Paddy's Pub T-shirts floating in it
jokes.setup: The gang is in crisis mode about an environmental dumping incident
jokes.punchline: The sheer specificity of their guilt — 500 gallons AND branded T-shirts as evidence — is so self-incriminating it's absurd
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny cold-open escalation: they're not denying guilt, just panicking about exposure, and the branded T-shirts as incriminating evidence is a sharp, specific detail that tells you everything about these idiots.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: you might want to jot down how well you're being treated at this professional establishment

jokes.text: "You might want to jot down how well you're being treated at this professional establishment."
jokes.setup: The gang is in full panic mode about an environmental scandal; Dennis steps away to corral the others
jokes.punchline: Dennis can't resist managing optics even mid-crisis, telling the potential reporter to note how well she's being treated — hilariously delusional self-promotion
jokes.explanation: Very Dennis — his narcissistic need to control perception overrides all rational crisis management. The gap between how dire the situation is and his PR instinct is what sells it. Strong character integration.

dialogue.line: Because they found 500 gallons of baby oil dumped in the Schuylkill River

jokes.text: Dennis: 'This is a good thing. This could be our Paddy's-gate.' Mac: 'No, but gates aren't a good thing. I mean, Pizzagate, Watergate.' Everyone: 'Nipplegate. Nipplegate.'
jokes.setup: Dennis enthusiastically frames a scandal as a branding opportunity
jokes.punchline: The gang derails into agreeing that gate-scandals are bad, then unanimously fixates on Nipplegate and Janet Jackson
jokes.explanation: The pivot from crisis management to nostalgia about Nipplegate is perfectly in-character. Dennis's oblivious reframing of a scandal as good PR is classic Dennis delusion, and the universal chorus of 'Nipplegate' shows the gang's shared idiocy.

dialogue.line: Well, the 200 Paddy's pub T-shirts floating around in it aren't exactly helping our case

jokes.text: "Well, the 200 Paddy's pub T-shirts floating around in it aren't exactly helping our case, pal."
jokes.setup: Dee suggests they can't be proved responsible for the baby oil dump
jokes.punchline: Their own branded merchandise is floating in the contaminated river — they branded the crime scene
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of the absurdity — not only did they dump 500 gallons of baby oil, they left branded T-shirts in it. The specificity of 200 shirts and 'pal' at the end adds contempt. Well-structured punchline.

dialogue.line: This could be our Paddy's-gate

jokes.text: 'Janet Jackson's career was never the same.' 'Some things you gotta keep covered up.'
jokes.setup: Sympathetic discussion of Janet Jackson's Nipplegate fallout
jokes.punchline: The lesson they draw from it — 'some things you gotta keep covered up' — applies directly to their own cover-up situation, which they're oblivious to
jokes.explanation: The double meaning is clean — they're literally advising themselves without knowing it. Functional irony, though not especially sharp by Sunny standards.

dialogue.line: Nipplegate. Janet Jackson's career was never the same

jokes.text: 'We didn't go to the retreat so much as watched clips of it on YouTube, but, you know, you're right, Mac.'
jokes.setup: Mac invokes the corporate retreat as the source of their new professional skills
jokes.punchline: Dennis casually corrects that they just watched YouTube clips but validates the point anyway
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the entire joke is delivered in one subordinate clause. Dennis's breezy, matter-of-fact correction that reveals the entire basis of their corporate competence is a lie is a great character beat. The 'but you're right, Mac' sells it.

dialogue.line: We didn't go to the retreat so much as watched clips of it on YouTube

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Normally a situation like this would have me clawing all your faces off. But I'm not gonna do that. I'm gonna utilize my words.'
jokes.setup: Dennis announces he's going to handle the crisis professionally using his corporate retreat training
jokes.punchline: His baseline is 'clawing faces off,' which he presents as the rational alternative he's heroically suppressing
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific joke. The juxtaposition of 'clawing faces off' with the corporate buzzword 'utilize my words' perfectly encapsulates the show's premise — these are feral people cosplaying as professionals. The delivery of 'I'm gonna utilize my words' as a heroic declaration is especially sharp.

dialogue.line: I do see your hand is still in a bit of a claw

jokes.text: The reveal that multiple gang members had their hands hidden in claw positions, ready to attack during the meeting
jokes.setup: Dennis announces they're going to handle things professionally
jokes.punchline: He and others reveal they had clawed hands hidden behind their heads/legs, ready to pounce
jokes.explanation: The visual of the entire gang having independently hidden claw hands during their professional conversation is a great physical gag. 'I had it hidden behind my head. I was ready to pounce' — the specificity makes it funnier. Rewatch bonus because you catch new details.

dialogue.line: I was ready to pounce. I had it hidden behind my head

jokes.text: 'We've got these awesome fleece vests inspired by the retreat... You can let it all go under here.'
jokes.setup: Mac lists the tools they've gained from the corporate retreat
jokes.punchline: The crowning achievement is matching fleece vests, and Dennis's 'you can let it all go under here' implies they're hiding things in the vest
jokes.explanation: The vests as the tangible output of corporate retreat cosplay is funny, with the implication that 'letting it all go under here' means concealing their true selves (or weapons). Decent character work, slightly underdeveloped.

dialogue.line: You can let it all go under here

jokes.text: Dennis says 'sacrificial lamb' and Charlie responds by discussing eating actual lamb and whether it would be tender and delicious
jokes.setup: Dennis uses the corporate metaphor 'a lamb, if you will' to propose a fall person
jokes.punchline: Charlie completely misses the metaphor and earnestly discusses whether eating lamb is a priority given their current problems
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. Charlie's literal-minded interpretation of 'lamb' as actual food is pitch-perfect character comedy — he's not stupid, just operates on a different frequency. 'Tender and delicious, but we have bigger issues' and 'eating lamb is not the best thing, momentarily speaking' are genuinely funny lines. The 'momentarily speaking' qualifies the lamb eating as merely a timing issue, not a bad idea in principle. Strongly character-integrated — only Charlie delivers this.

dialogue.line: Yes, a lamb if you will

jokes.text: "Thank you for pointing out that gender inequity, Dee. And, henceforth, let's refer to that position as 'fall person.'"
jokes.setup: Dee notes the phrase is 'fall guy' not 'fall gal'
jokes.punchline: Dennis adopts corporate-speak woke language ('gender inequity,' 'henceforth') while still planning to scapegoat Dee — the progressive framing is immediately weaponized against her
jokes.explanation: Good satirical jab at corporate performative inclusivity — the language of equity deployed to more elegantly scapegoat Dee. The irony is sharp and character-specific to Dennis.

dialogue.line: that lamb right now could be tender and delicious, but we have kind of bigger issues

jokes.text: '...or even fall bird, and then we're back to Dee.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is offering animal-based neutral alternatives to 'fall guy'
jokes.punchline: He lands on 'fall bird' and immediately clocks that birds = Dee (a long-running nickname insult), bringing it full circle
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. Charlie's journey from 'fall fish' to 'scapefish' to 'fall bird' — and then the instantaneous, matter-of-fact realization that 'fall bird' means Dee — is a masterclass in comedic economy. The structure is perfect: build absurdity, then collapse it into the most specific and cruel punchline possible. 'And then we're back to Dee' has the casual devastation of a perfect roast line. It's a callback to years of bird insults AND a logical argument completion simultaneously. Near-flawless.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I would like to respectfully point out that the phrase is fall 'guy'

jokes.text: Mac: 'Oh, gosh, I'm so sorry guys, but my hand is so tightly clenched into a claw.' Everyone agrees theirs is too.
jokes.setup: The gang has been trying to unlearn their claw-hands as part of corporate professionalism
jokes.punchline: The 'fall bird' insult toward Dee causes everyone's hands to involuntarily re-claw
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff — the claw returns as a measure of emotional regulation failure. Mac's apologetic 'oh gosh, I'm so sorry' before announcing his hand is a claw is a funny formulation. The gag has escalation built in.

dialogue.line: We could consider 'fall fish,' uh, or 'scapefish' or even 'fall bird,' and then we're back to Dee

jokes.text: The jug argument: Frank finds a jug out back, the gang immediately argues about whether you blow on it or bang on it as an instrument
jokes.setup: The gang discovers a jug and needs to decide what to do with it
jokes.punchline: The crisis begins not with any real decision but with a violent argument about the correct way to play a jug as an instrument
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny origin story energy — the entire catastrophe begins with an argument so stupid and irrelevant it's beautiful. The gang's ability to escalate from 'found a jug' to 'vigorous clawing' over musical technique establishes the episode's flashback perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: my hand is so tightly clenched into a claw

jokes.text: 'That led to a vigorous debate, which in turn led to vigorous clawing until we decided to stop fighting and simply get our own jugs.'
jokes.setup: Dennis narrates the origin story in corporate-speak
jokes.punchline: The 'vigorous clawing' as a business process step, narrated with complete matter-of-factness, is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'Vigorous clawing' as a neutral business-narration term is excellent. The corporate framing of their feral behavior is the episode's core joke engine and this is a clean execution of it.

dialogue.line: No, you make sounds when you bang on it, not blow on it

jokes.text: "Annoyingly, however, the jugs were filled with fluid." / "Yeah, can't really play them as an instrument until we..."
jokes.setup: They each got their own jugs; now they have a new problem
jokes.punchline: The jugs came filled with water, which is an inconvenience — they never considered this — and must be emptied before jug music can commence
jokes.explanation: Funny because water in a water jug is treated as an unexpected obstacle. The logic is airtight in its absurdity — of course the jugs have fluid — and 'annoyingly' captures their entitled frustration perfectly.

dialogue.line: Uh, you don't wanna wash the bar with a... with a water-based liquid

jokes.text: The gang discovers the jugs are filled with fluid and debates what to do — suggestions include washing the bar with it, making a fire to put out, and playing the jugs
jokes.setup: The jugs are filled with fluid, so they can't be played as instruments
jokes.punchline: Frank proposes making a fire specifically so they have a reason to use the liquid; the idea that they'd create a problem to solve it is treated as reasonable
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'make a fire and put it out' logic — creating a problem to justify a solution — is very in-character and funny. The practical absurdism of the gang's brainstorming is well-executed, though the crosstalk makes it slightly muddy.

dialogue.line: So we have a reason to use all this liquid

jokes.text: 'After an hour-long argument about the best way to dispose of the fluid, we caved and decided the best way to make the jugs empty was to simply drink the water.'
jokes.setup: An hour of creative alternatives to water disposal
jokes.punchline: The revolutionary solution: drink the water
jokes.explanation: The punchline is the deadpan escalation — after an hour of increasingly absurd proposals, 'simply drink the water' as the genius solution they 'caved' to is a perfect comedic reversal. The word 'caved' implies this was a capitulation rather than the obvious answer.

dialogue.line: Now if I'm braising something, is that a way to cook something, or is that shellacking it?

jokes.text: Charlie's watercooler conversation: 'Now if I'm braising something, is that a way to cook something, or is that shellacking it? Like, am I putting sauce on it?'
jokes.setup: The watercooler is described as spawning organic workplace conversation and 'health initiatives'
jokes.punchline: Charlie's contribution to the think tank is fundamental confusion about basic cooking vocabulary
jokes.explanation: Charlie conflating 'braising' with 'shellacking' is a good Charlie-specific detail — he's genuinely confused about a mundane thing in a very specific way. 'Is that shellacking it?' as an alternative culinary term is a funny wrong word.

dialogue.line: you can actually put a tablespoon of baby oil in your coffee in the morning and it resets the pH balance of your gut biome

jokes.text: Frank: 'You can actually put a tablespoon of baby oil in your coffee in the morning and it resets the pH balance of your gut biome.' Dennis: 'You drink it?'
jokes.setup: Frank confidently delivers wellness advice about baby oil consumption
jokes.punchline: Dennis's minimal, incredulous 'You drink it?' sells the absurdity without overcrowding it
jokes.explanation: The two-word response 'You drink it?' is a masterclass in comedic economy. Frank's confident wellness misinformation about baby oil in coffee — framed as insider knowledge — is perfectly absurd, and Dennis's reaction (not repulsed, just confused about the delivery method) is exactly right. The joke trusts the audience. Dennis doesn't say 'that's insane,' just 'you drink it' — implying baby oil on the outside of a person is fine, but IN the coffee is the weird part.

dialogue.line: if you're gonna dump stuff, the best place is the ocean. I mean, you know, in a pinch, you go to a lake or a river

jokes.text: Frank: 'If you're gonna dump stuff, the best place is the ocean. In a pinch, go to a lake or a river.'
jokes.setup: Watercooler conversation at Paddy's Pub
jokes.punchline: Frank casually shares his professional hierarchy for illegal dumping as though it's common knowledge advice
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines. Frank's casual, authoritative ranking of environmental dumping locations — delivered as practical advice over a watercooler — is perfect dark comedy. 'In a pinch, go to a lake or a river' implies he has a whole ethical framework around illegal dumping. The economy is exceptional; it's also foreshadowing for the episode's central crime.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Dennis, how do they get the oil out of the baby?

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Dennis, how do they get the oil out of the baby? Do they have to mash the babies up or grind them? Is it babies that are sick and dying already, or what is the oil...' Dennis: 'Don't be an idiot, Charlie. The babies are alive. They just wring them out like an old rag.'
jokes.setup: Frank mentions using baby oil exclusively after showers
jokes.punchline: Charlie asks how the oil is extracted from babies; Dennis doesn't question the premise — he corrects Charlie's inefficient grinding/mashing method and specifies they're wrung out like rags while alive
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode by a wide margin. The structure is perfect: Charlie asks the wrong (but internally logical) question, and Dennis's response doesn't correct the false premise — he only corrects the method. 'Don't be an idiot, Charlie. The babies are alive. They just wring them out like an old rag.' Dennis's confidence and specificity make it. He's not horrified by the concept — he's annoyed at Charlie's ignorance. The 'like an old rag' simile is the killer detail. This is the kind of dark absurdist beat that made Always Sunny legendary — it escalates past the obvious joke into something genuinely disturbing and hilarious simultaneously. Approaches the calibration anchor territory.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: They just wring them out like an old rag

jokes.text: "Don't be an idiot, Charlie. The babies are alive. They just wring them out like an old rag."
jokes.setup: Charlie asks if the babies used for baby oil are sick and dying
jokes.punchline: Dennis corrects him — the babies are alive and you just wring them — said with complete authority and mild irritation at Charlie's ignorance
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and easily the most quotable. Dennis correcting Charlie's wrong baby oil theory with an even more horrifying wrong answer, delivered with complete authority and mild contempt, is a masterclass in dark comedy. 'Like an old rag' is a perfect simile. The joke works because Dennis isn't being intentionally dark — he genuinely believes this and is annoyed Charlie didn't know. Very comparable to the vasectomy anchor example in its escalation and character specificity.

dialogue.line: it's like a rhombus on wheels

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis's passionate defense of the Cybertruck: 'It delivers on the promise of the future from our youth... Hard lines, sharp corners, DeLorean-like materials... It's the transportation fitting of a Terminator.'
jokes.setup: Watercooler conversation pivots to the Cybertruck
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis are united in a weirdly passionate, specific nostalgia-fueled love for the Cybertruck, connecting it to childhood promises of the future
jokes.explanation: The Cybertruck love is funny as a character detail — Mac and Dennis's shared aesthetic sensibility around aggressive masculinity and 'future promises' is well-observed. 'Transportation fitting of a Terminator' is a good line. Serves more as setup for later payoffs than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: slap fighting is the future of dispute mitigation

jokes.text: 'Yeah, it's like a rhombus on wheels.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are enthusiastically describing the Cybertruck's futuristic design
jokes.punchline: Charlie reduces the entire aesthetic vision to 'a rhombus on wheels,' which is both accurate and completely deflating
jokes.explanation: Four words that puncture Mac and Dennis's entire passionate Cybertruck monologue. It's accurate — the Cybertruck IS basically a rhombus — and Charlie says it as agreement, not mockery, which makes it funnier. Perfect economy.

dialogue.line: We were using it to-to-to settle arguments. We were using it to end the day, to start the day, to say goodbye, to say hello...to celebrate, to mourn

jokes.text: 'Just like the Cybertruck is the future of transportation, slap fighting is the future of dispute mitigation.'
jokes.setup: Watercooler discussion about the Cybertruck
jokes.punchline: Mac pivots from admiring the Cybertruck to pitching slap fighting as a business concept, using the Cybertruck as rhetorical scaffolding
jokes.explanation: 'Dispute mitigation' as corporate-speak for slapping people is excellent. The parallel construction with Cybertruck gives Mac's pitch a false logical architecture. Very in-character for Mac to frame violence as innovation.

dialogue.line: We were all slapped across the proverbial cheeks with this venture

jokes.text: Cut to: 'The Egyptians, they like the cats. Yeah. I know, but it's a cat-based society, you know what I mean?'
jokes.setup: 'My God, was he right. We had to try our hand at it.'
jokes.punchline: Instead of showing slap fighting excitement, we cut to Charlie earnestly explaining ancient Egyptian cat culture mid-conversation
jokes.explanation: The watercooler-to-Egyptian-cats jump cut is a great comedic non-sequitur. The juxtaposition of Mac's visionary pitch against Charlie earnestly lecturing about cat-based ancient societies captures the gang's ADD perfectly. 'It's a cat-based society, you know what I mean?' is a funny way to put it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: you can stick this line of logic up your various assholes

jokes.text: Mac's business pitch for professional slap fighting, followed by the visual of the guys slapping the shit out of each other and someone yelling 'Take your shirts off!'
jokes.setup: Mac pivots slap fighting into a formal business venture
jokes.punchline: The immediate chaos and someone shouting 'Take your shirts off' mid-slap fight reveals this 'professional' venture is just barely-structured mayhem
jokes.explanation: 'Take your shirts off!' as the first adjustment to make slap fighting more professional is very on-brand for the gang's particular brand of eroticism-adjacent male bonding. Physical comedy inferred from context.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: But chick saturation has gone down

jokes.text: "Oh, shit. Take your shirts off, though. Whoa!"
jokes.setup: The gang is seeing slap fighting for the first time, apparently watching something impressive
jokes.punchline: Their visceral reaction — shirts coming off — implies they're watching a slap fight and immediately become both excited and aroused
jokes.explanation: Physical reaction beat that gets the job done. The boys immediately wanting to remove shirts at the sight of slap fighting is consistent character work but not a standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: At a certain point, we stopped women from going wild. Why did we do that?

jokes.text: Mac resists being named the fall person, then directly states: 'I'd like to add, you can stick this line of logic up your various assholes.'
jokes.setup: Everyone seemingly agrees Mac is the logical fall person
jokes.punchline: Mac drops the corporate veneer and tells them to shove it 'up your various assholes' — 'various' is the key word
jokes.explanation: 'Various assholes' is the corporate-language bleed into vulgarity — 'various' is a business report word applied to anatomy. The structure works because he was playing along with the meeting's professional register until this crack. Dennis's 'that's harsher language than I thought we were allowed to use here' acknowledges the register break while still being in-the-bit.

dialogue.line: They're too dry, and so they don't feel wild

jokes.text: "So, Mac is clearly the prime candidate to fall on the metaphorical sword here. Yes?" — everyone agrees immediately
jokes.setup: The gang has laid out how Mac's slap fighting idea led to all the problems
jokes.punchline: Everyone agrees Mac should take the fall — immediately, unanimously, with no pushback — which is funny given they're supposed to be fair about it
jokes.explanation: The speed of the agreement is funny — the corporate deliberation process they've set up collapses instantly when it's time to actually deliberate. Standard Sunny dynamic, well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: My personal distaste for women aside, I think you crapped the bed on the execution

jokes.text: Dennis's presentation: 'Slaps and profits have gone up. That's great. But chick saturation has gone down. That's not good. The whole thing is sorely lacking eroticism. The data is alarming.'
jokes.setup: Dennis presents his business analysis of the slap fighting venture
jokes.punchline: 'Chick saturation' as a KPI, 'eroticism' as a business metric tracked via data, all delivered with the gravity of a quarterly earnings call
jokes.explanation: 'Chick saturation' and 'The data is alarming' applied to a lack of eroticism is brilliant Dennis characterization. Only Dennis Reynolds would have a data-driven approach to the erotic content of his bar's fight club. 'The data is alarming' in particular is a great line — gravely serious about something deeply sexist and absurd. This scores high because it's completely Dennis-specific, the corporate framing adds rather than decorates, and 'chick saturation' is a genuinely inventive term.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: you're coming at me open-kimono here

jokes.text: Dennis: 'We were promised mud wrestling. We were promised wet T-shirt contests. We were promised women going wild. At a certain point, we stopped women from going wild. Why did we do that? They wanna go wild. Let's let them go wild. They're too dry, and so they don't feel wild.'
jokes.setup: Dennis pivots his business pitch from slap fighting metrics to cultural grievance
jokes.punchline: The escalating catalog of 1990s male gaze nostalgia — mud wrestling, wet T-shirts, women going wild — culminates in 'they're too dry, and so they don't feel wild'
jokes.explanation: Dennis's grievance monologue about unfulfilled cultural promises of eroticism is excellent character work. 'They're too dry, and so they don't feel wild' is a killer punchline — it's completely illogical as a sociological argument while making perfect internal sense to Dennis. The speech escalates beautifully to that final line. Deeply Dennis.

dialogue.line: They'll bite you

jokes.text: 'There is an underserved market for one-on-one erotic sport competition between scantily-clad, oiled-up women.'
jokes.setup: Dennis's business pitch for the new direction
jokes.punchline: He frames his personal sexual fantasy as a gap in the market, using business-speak to launder the creepiness
jokes.explanation: Dennis presenting his fantasies as market research is classic Dennis. 'Underserved market' as framing for 'thing I personally want to see' is funny corporate-speak, and 'erotic sport competition' is a good euphemism.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Back in the day when we were taking down all the aluminum siding, what are we gonna do with all that asbestos that was left? We dumped it in the Schuylkill

jokes.text: Frank: 'My personal distaste for women aside, I think you crapped the bed on the execution.'
jokes.setup: Frank is critiquing Dennis's business idea
jokes.punchline: He casually announces 'my personal distaste for women aside' as though it's a neutral qualifier before delivering his critique
jokes.explanation: 'My personal distaste for women aside' is a Frank line for the ages. The structure is perfect — it's delivered as a formal disclaimer before a business critique, as if woman-distaste is a standard conflict-of-interest to disclose. The economy is exceptional: five words reveal an entire character dimension while functioning as a throat-clearing placeholder. It's deeply Frank-specific and completely unexpected. High quotability.

dialogue.line: Yeah. Well, and you never will see 'em, Frank. Because there's only one single headlight

jokes.text: 'You're coming at me open-kimono here, and I appreciate that, so kudos... But I do think we need to helicopter up, stretch the vantage point a little bit. I think we need to chew on the key protein here, which I believe to be Dee.'
jokes.setup: Dennis deflects blame for the first time
jokes.punchline: Three consecutive corporate buzzword metaphors ('open-kimono,' 'helicopter up,' 'key protein') culminate in pointing the finger at Dee
jokes.explanation: 'Key protein' as a business term for 'fall person' is funny — implying Dee is nourishment for their corporate survival strategy. The stacked buzzwords satirize corporate-speak well, though it's perhaps one metaphor too many.

dialogue.line: The lower the self-esteem, the harder the slap. And Dee could take a hit too. Years of getting slapped around by Frank

jokes.text: "You know, you're coming at me open-kimono here, and I appreciate that, so kudos."
jokes.setup: Frank has just criticized Dennis's business plan and nominated him as the fall person
jokes.punchline: Dennis responds with corporate-speak ('open-kimono' meaning total transparency) and a 'kudos' — praising Frank for the attack on him
jokes.explanation: 'Open-kimono' is real corporate jargon deployed well here. The 'kudos' is funny — Dennis's ego requires him to give praise even when receiving criticism. Solid character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Well, I am your sister

jokes.text: On why the women slappers are unsatisfactory: 'What? They're ugly.' 'They're ugly.' 'I didn't wanna say it, but they are ugly.' 'They're a bit gruff, aren't they?'
jokes.setup: Discussion of why the erotic slap fighting venture isn't achieving 'erotic escape velocity'
jokes.punchline: The elaborate buildup to what's wrong yields 'they're ugly' — delivered in cascading agreement
jokes.explanation: The cascading agreement ('I didn't wanna say it, but they are ugly') is the structure here — the joke is the chorus of agreement, not the insult itself. 'A bit gruff' as the euphemistic version is a nice Frank touch. Functional but not elevated.

dialogue.speaker: The Waitress
dialogue.line: Are you stalking me again?

jokes.text: 'The big issue for me is you can't put baby oil on any of these women. They'll bite you. I had one almost bend my arm completely in half. I tried to put baby oil on her and she...' 'I got pinned by her too, man.'
jokes.setup: Discussion of the inadequate attractiveness of their current slap fighters
jokes.punchline: Their approach to assessing the women is to try to oil them — and they were defeated in the attempt
jokes.explanation: The idea that Mac's quality-control test for female fighters is trying to apply baby oil — and that the women beat him up for it — is a funny reversal. 'She almost bent my arm completely in half' as a complaint about a woman he was trying to oil against her will is dark and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Since when did I ever stalk you? No, that's not my thing. Flirting, maybe

jokes.text: Frank recalls luring women with a Cadillac while disposing of asbestos from aluminum siding in the Schuylkill River as a business precedent
jokes.setup: The gang brainstorms how to attract more attractive women to the slap fighting event
jokes.punchline: Frank's relevant experience involves dumping asbestos from aluminum siding into the same river — this is not his first environmental crime there
jokes.explanation: The casual revelation that Frank has previously dumped asbestos in the Schuylkill while luring women with a Cadillac as a corporate precedent is very Frank. Deepens his character as a career criminal while advancing the plot logic.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: Little did he know that she wasn't just driving that crappy car, she was living in it

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Everybody needs money.' Dennis: 'Wait. I know exactly what we should do.' Charlie: 'Oh! I was thinking the same thing.' Dennis: 'I doubt it.'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to participate in the planning
jokes.punchline: Dennis flatly says 'I doubt it' to Charlie's claim that he had the same idea
jokes.explanation: 'I doubt it' — two words that perfectly express Dennis's condescension toward Charlie. Good economy, good character beat. Not original but cleanly executed.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Cybertruck not included. Can you read?

jokes.text: Frank reveals the prize: a Cybertruck. The gang marvels at its hard angles.
jokes.setup: The gang needs to lure attractive women to their slap fighting event
jokes.punchline: Frank produces a Cybertruck, which the gang immediately reveres with the same 'hard angles' language used earlier
jokes.explanation: The callback to the watercooler Cybertruck worship pays off — Frank actually bought one. 'Look at the hard angles on this' echoing the earlier conversation is satisfying structural craft.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Frank was growing in hardness as the eroticism in the bar was increasing. And, uh, he was becoming as hard as a Cybertruck himself

jokes.text: "I can't wait to see the headlights on her." / "Yeah, well, and you never will see 'em, Frank. Because there's only one single headlight."
jokes.setup: The gang sees an outstanding female slapper they want to recruit
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'headlights' comment is a crude double entendre; Dennis corrects him that the Cybertruck literally only has one headlight — the sexual innuendo is killed by automotive accuracy
jokes.explanation: Smart double-meaning joke that undercuts the innuendo with literal automotive fact. Dennis correcting Frank's innuendo with Cybertruck specs is both funny and very character-specific — Dennis's obsession with accuracy. The misdirection is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yo, baby. I need a prostitute

jokes.text: 'I can't wait to see the headlights on her.' 'Yeah!' 'Well, and you never will see 'em, Frank. Because there's only one single headlight.' 'Oh.'
jokes.setup: Frank's sexually charged comment about a woman fighter they can't take their eyes off
jokes.punchline: Dennis corrects the double entendre: she literally only has one headlight (eye), making Frank's creepy comment more innocent while making the woman more unusual
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection — Frank's 'I can't wait to see the headlights on her' is clearly sexual, but Dennis's correction is literal. The 'Oh.' from Frank — brief, unreadable — is a great reaction beat. The reveal that she has one eye also retroactively explains why 'we couldn't take our eyes off her.'

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Um, also, there's still a bunch of dudes in the basement

jokes.text: 'Dee was tearing through girls like a paper shredder through company records. And we knew she would, as I had explained it with a graph. The lower the self-esteem, the harder the slap.'
jokes.setup: Dennis narrates Dee's success in the slap fighting tournament
jokes.punchline: 'Like a paper shredder through company records' and the low self-esteem graph are both savage, and the graph correlating Dee's low self-esteem to slapping power is both cruel and logically coherent
jokes.explanation: 'Paper shredder through company records' is a great corporate metaphor applied to violence, and 'the lower the self-esteem, the harder the slap' as an actual business graph is both a devastating Dee insult and a weirdly plausible pseudo-scientific finding. The graph is Dennis at his peak: systematizing cruelty into data. High marks for character integration — this is completely Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Eleven. Eleven. Eleven's the answer

jokes.text: "Dee was tearing through girls like a paper shredder through company records."
jokes.setup: Dee is dominating the slap competition
jokes.punchline: Dennis's narrator simile — 'paper shredder through company records' — is both apt for Dee's destruction AND a dark callback to their earlier corporate crimes (they'd need to shred records)
jokes.explanation: Very well-crafted simile that works on two levels: describes Dee's physical efficiency and nods at the gang's own record-shredding instincts. The corporate metaphor applied to violence is the episode's consistent comic mode and this is one of its best executions.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I thought it was an aquatic vehicle

jokes.text: Mac: 'Right? Years of getting slapped around by Frank, right?' Frank: 'Yeah. Those were the days.' Mac: 'If you say so, buddy. If you say so.'
jokes.setup: Dennis explains Dee can take a hit because of her upbringing
jokes.punchline: Frank's nostalgic 'those were the days' about hitting Dee as a child, and Mac's weary 'if you say so' as the only response
jokes.explanation: 'Those were the days' as Frank's reaction to child abuse reminiscence is perfectly dark. Mac's 'if you say so' is the right amount of weary acceptance — not horrified, not endorsing, just tired. This is Sunny at its darkest and most character-specific.

dialogue.line: It should be, but it's not

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Dee, I thank you for your service. I love you like a sister.' Dee: 'Well, I am your sister.' Dennis: 'Well, you know, familial ties notwithstanding.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is diplomatically sidelining Dee after she got knocked out
jokes.punchline: 'Familial ties notwithstanding' as a qualifier for 'I love you like a sister' — when she IS his sister — implies the familial tie doesn't actually create any affection
jokes.explanation: The structure is tight: Dennis uses 'love you like a sister' as a corporate-speak platitude, Dee correctly points out the literal truth, and Dennis's 'familial ties notwithstanding' acknowledges and immediately discounts the actual relationship. The implication — that being literally his sister doesn't actually make him love her — is devastating and perfectly Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I think the truck is ugly

jokes.text: "Dee, I thank you for your service. I love you like a sister. Well, I am your sister. Well, you know, familial ties notwithstanding."
jokes.setup: Dee has been knocked out and is being consoled/dismissed
jokes.punchline: Dennis says 'I love you like a sister,' Dee corrects that she IS his sister, and Dennis immediately qualifies with 'familial ties notwithstanding' — his affection is entirely conditional and corporate
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis joke. The 'I love you like a sister' / 'I am your sister' / 'familial ties notwithstanding' beat is tight and devastating. The 'notwithstanding' caveat means he's actively discounting the actual familial relationship. Three beats in quick succession, all landing. Very quotable, strong character integration.

dialogue.line: Yes, hammer down on our brand identity and come out open commando

jokes.text: 'I think you've proven yourself to be pretty good at taking a fall.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is diplomatically releasing Dee from the slap fighting venture after she got knocked out
jokes.punchline: He means she's literally good at being knocked down, then pivots it to suggest she should be the fall person
jokes.explanation: Decent double-meaning — literally taking physical falls vs. being the corporate scapegoat. Clean construction, though not especially surprising at this point in the episode.

dialogue.line: I'm sorry, do you think I'm a reporter? No. I'm here for the orgy

jokes.text: Dee: 'I think we're styling the wrong mannequin here.' Dennis: 'What?' Dee: 'I would have won that competition if it wasn't for our associate deviating from the business plan, and that would be Charlie.'
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to deflect blame using corporate buzzwords
jokes.punchline: 'Styling the wrong mannequin' is a malapropism/invented corporate phrase that makes no sense, and everyone ignores it
jokes.explanation: 'Styling the wrong mannequin' is a good fake corporate buzzword — it sounds like it means something but doesn't. Dee's adoption of the meeting's language while deflecting to Charlie is in-character.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh. Hey, guys, the whore is here

jokes.text: Charlie recruits the Waitress: 'We're doing these oiled-up slap fights in the bar.' Waitress: 'So I could oil you or you could oil yourself, but...' Waitress: 'Did you come here to ask me if I want to get oiled by you? Are you stalking me again?'
jokes.setup: Charlie approaches the Waitress with his business pitch
jokes.punchline: The pitch is so creepy it immediately triggers a stalking accusation; Charlie's response ('Flirting, maybe. But...') is the reveal
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie/Waitress dynamic. 'Did you come here to ask me if I want to get oiled by you?' is a great line because it accurately summarizes what Charlie did. Charlie's correction — 'Stalking? Since when did I ever stalk you? Flirting, maybe' — is a perfect character beat that acknowledges his behavior without comprehending it.

dialogue.line: That's not an orgy. That's a gangbang

jokes.text: Charlie shows the Waitress the Cybertruck prize. She's initially unimpressed, then: 'You're giving away a truck? A Cybertruck?' Mmm. Cut to: she's living in her car.
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to sell the Waitress on the slap fighting prize truck
jokes.punchline: Her 'Mmm' of interest is immediately explained — she's living in a car, so the prize is life-changing for her
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the Waitress is living in her car — and the dark irony that the gang's creepy enterprise is her best shot at housing — is both funny and genuinely bleak in the best Sunny tradition. The structure is perfect: her 'Mmm' is intriguing, then the cut explains everything. Good rewatch value because on second viewing you clock the car she's driving as her home.

jokes.text: "Little did he know that she wasn't just driving that crappy car, she was living in it." — reveal of The Waitress living in her car
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to lure The Waitress with the Cybertruck prize; she seems resistant
jokes.punchline: She's actually homeless and living in her car — the Cybertruck isn't just a cool prize, it's a life necessity — which makes Charlie's oblivious flirting much darker
jokes.explanation: Good dark reveal. 'Little did he know' is a classic narrator undercut. The Waitress being homeless adds dark stakes that reframe her earlier hesitation and makes her subsequent domination more satisfying and tragic. Well-timed reveal.

jokes.text: 'The allure of the Cybertruck and a lifetime of petty misery suffered by this woman rendered her unstoppable.'
jokes.setup: The Waitress enters the slap fighting tournament
jokes.punchline: Dennis narrates her success by crediting 'a lifetime of petty misery' as her competitive advantage
jokes.explanation: 'A lifetime of petty misery' is a beautifully concise summary of the Waitress's character arc across the entire series. The word 'petty' doing a lot of work — not tragic misery, just the small grinding kind. Excellent economy, very quotable.

jokes.text: Charlie tries to negotiate a tie with the Waitress mid-fight: 'What if you and I get a little side pot going, we tone down on the slaps, we call it a tie, and that way we can share the Cyber...' She immediately slaps him full force.
jokes.setup: Charlie enters the fight and immediately tries to negotiate out of competing
jokes.punchline: He doesn't even finish his pitch before she slaps the shit out of him
jokes.explanation: The mid-sentence interruption by slap is a great comedic beat. Charlie's gambit — negotiating a share of the prize by offering to throw the fight — reveals his usual cowardice and scheming, and the Waitress's response of simply slapping him while he's still talking is perfect.

jokes.text: "What if you and I get a little side pot going, right? W-What if you and I... we tone down on the slaps, we call it a tie, and that way we can share the Cyber..." — she immediately slaps him
jokes.setup: Charlie is facing The Waitress in the slap competition; he tries to propose a deal to share the truck
jokes.punchline: He doesn't even finish the sentence before she slaps him flat — she needs that truck and his charm offensive has zero effect
jokes.explanation: Great physical comedy beat with perfect character logic — Charlie's attempt to use their 'connection' to game the competition is immediately demolished. The Waitress's silent, immediate slap mid-sentence is funnier than any verbal punchline. The physical comedy and character dynamic work together perfectly.

jokes.text: Charlie's post-fight excuse: 'I was sucker-punched.' Mac/Dennis: 'No. No. Mm-mmm.' Charlie: 'No. You were looking right at her.' Charlie: 'She slapped the shit out of me, but I wasn't ready. It was uncalled for and it wasn't fair.'
jokes.setup: Charlie lost his fight with the Waitress
jokes.punchline: He claims sucker-punch while having been directly facing her; then the even more pathetic 'it was uncalled for and it wasn't fair' in a slap FIGHTING context
jokes.explanation: 'It was uncalled for and it wasn't fair' about losing a slap fighting competition he voluntarily entered is excellent wounded dignity comedy. 'You were looking right at her' as the counter-argument is devastating.

jokes.text: Frank shows Waitress the fine print: 'Cybertruck not included. Can you read?' Waitress: 'Oh my God!' Frank: 'In plain writing.'
jokes.setup: The Waitress wins the slap fighting competition and expects her Cybertruck
jokes.punchline: Frank refuses to give the prize, citing 'Cybertruck not included' in the terms and conditions, and smugly asks 'Can you read?'
jokes.explanation: 'Can you read?' as Frank's smug response to defrauding a homeless woman is perfectly in character. The T&C loophole is a classic Frank move. The double 'Can you read?' adds the right twist of condescension.

jokes.text: Charlie attempts corporate speak: 'ear-wise, you're giving me various wordables that are adding up to thoughts.'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to participate in the professional meeting format
jokes.punchline: 'Wordables' as Charlie's invented corporate noun — words as 'ables' that are 'adding up to thoughts' — reveals he has absorbed the form but not the content of corporate language
jokes.explanation: 'Wordables' is a genuinely inventive piece of Charlie's idiosyncratic language. 'Ear-wise' as a qualifier, 'mouth-wise' following it, and 'wordables adding up to thoughts' — this is Charlie at his most Charlie. He's correctly identified that corporate-speak adds '-able' and '-ize' to things and runs with it in the wrong direction. Very quotable and highly character-specific.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'I see how you're trying to clip my wings so that I can fly.' Dennis: 'That's not how birds work. That makes them un-fly.' Charlie: 'Okay. I did not know that you were the bird expert.'
jokes.setup: Charlie uses a bird metaphor to frame how being blamed will help him
jokes.punchline: Dennis corrects the biology with 'that makes them un-fly' — a perfect deadpan refutation — and Charlie's comeback is to question his credentials
jokes.explanation: 'Un-fly' is an excellent invented word that perfectly refutes the metaphor on its own absurd terms. Dennis taking the metaphor literally to destroy it is a great comic structure. Charlie's indignant 'I did not know that you were the bird expert' — refusing to admit the metaphor doesn't work — is a perfect Charlie response.

jokes.text: Charlie's graph reveals Frank was 'growing in hardness' as bar eroticism increased, 'becoming as hard as a Cybertruck himself, which you could see.' Then: 'Cheese, of course, is also on this graph.'
jokes.setup: Charlie presents his data analysis of the erotic environment
jokes.punchline: The graph correlates Frank's arousal with bar eroticism AND cheese for reasons never explained, then immediately moves on
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Cheese, of course, is also on this graph' — delivered as a matter-of-fact parenthetical and immediately dropped — is structurally perfect absurdist comedy. The 'of course' is the key: it implies cheese's presence on an eroticism-arousal graph is self-evident, requiring no explanation. And it gets none. It's also the most Charlie possible data variable. The delivery of 'just keep going' / 'uh, moving past' shows even the other characters don't want to engage. Approaches the Snip-snap calibration zone for character-specific absurdism.

jokes.text: Charlie describes Frank's basement operation: 'I'm tryna say dudes were paying Frank to go into the basement... And he was failing in his efforts to poach talent from the slapping pool.'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to explain Frank's basement orgy operation using corporate language
jokes.punchline: 'Poach talent from the slapping pool' as a description of Frank trying to solicit women from the slap fighting event into his basement orgy is a perfect corporate euphemism
jokes.explanation: 'Poach talent from the slapping pool' describing solicitation for an orgy is a good euphemism. The HR language applied to Frank's sex work operation is consistently funny.

jokes.text: Frank's direct-to-potential-prostitute: 'Yo, baby. I need a prostitute.' Then: 'Well, when's she coming back from The Bahamas?'
jokes.setup: Charlie describes Frank trying to recruit for his basement orgy
jokes.punchline: Frank's approach is 'Yo, baby. I need a prostitute.' — maximally direct — and his follow-up question reveals even this approach failed
jokes.explanation: 'Yo, baby. I need a prostitute.' is a great Frank line — no pretense, no approach, pure transaction. The specificity of 'when's she coming back from The Bahamas?' as his follow-up reveals this particular person has a regular he's trying to reach, which adds a whole sad/absurd dimension. Economy is exceptional — four words tell you everything you need to know about Frank's approach to human interaction.

jokes.text: 'Also, there's still a bunch of dudes in the basement.' 'Yeah, there's like guys down there now.' 'How many are down there?' 'Eleven. Eleven. Eleven's the answer.'
jokes.setup: Frank's basement orgy has been implicated as a reason he panicked and dumped the Cybertruck
jokes.punchline: In the middle of their cover-up planning, Charlie reveals there are still eleven men in the basement right now — and states the number three times
jokes.explanation: The mid-crisis reveal of eleven basement men is a great escalation. 'Eleven. Eleven. Eleven's the answer.' — Charlie stating the number three times with increasing certainty is a funny delivery choice. The specificity of eleven (not five, not twenty) is correct.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I didn't know. I thought it was an aquatic vehicle.' Dennis/Charlie: 'It's an environmental nightmare.' Frank: 'It should be, but it's not. If anything, it looks like it goes into space.'
jokes.setup: Frank is accused of driving a Cybertruck into the river
jokes.punchline: Frank thought the Cybertruck was aquatic (consistent with his earlier 'it looks like it goes into space' logic), and when told it's an environmental nightmare he says 'it should be, but it's not'
jokes.explanation: 'I thought it was an aquatic vehicle' is a brilliant Frank excuse that makes internal sense — the Cybertruck DOES look like it could go underwater. 'It should be, but it's not' acknowledges the design implies it while denying the fact. Frank's confidence about his wrong interpretation is perfect.

jokes.text: "I gotta come clean. I think the truck is ugly."
jokes.setup: Frank says he has to 'come clean' — everyone expects a confession about the orgy or the dumping
jokes.punchline: Dee's 'coming clean' is that she thinks the Cybertruck is ugly — cutting against the entire gang's reverence throughout the episode
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode callback punchline. After 18 minutes of Cybertruck worship — the catalyst for the entire plot — Dee casually confesses it's ugly. The 'I gotta come clean' misdirection makes the reveal funnier. The gang's outrage ('Damn it. I knew it. Stupid. I call bullshit') is a great reaction. Well-structured payoff.

jokes.text: "Damn it. I knew you were gonna say that. I knew she was gonna say that. Stupid. You're stupid. I call bullshit on that."
jokes.setup: Dee reveals she thinks the Cybertruck is ugly
jokes.punchline: The gang's outrage over aesthetic Cybertruck opinion while they face serious criminal charges is hilariously misplaced priority
jokes.explanation: The reaction to Dee's Cybertruck opinion being treated as more serious than the actual crisis is funny but the joke is essentially the same as joke 71 — this is the echo, not the bell. Still lands well due to their collective outrage.

jokes.text: Dee drops the corporate veneer: 'I gotta come clean. I think the truck is ugly.' Dennis: 'Damn it. I knew you were gonna say that. Stupid. I call bullshit on that.'
jokes.setup: In the middle of serious cover-up deliberations, Dee takes the floor
jokes.punchline: Her big confession is a design opinion about the Cybertruck, which breaks Dennis and Mac's reverence — Dennis's 'I call bullshit on that' treated as though it's a factual claim
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff — Dee's mundane aesthetic opinion ('the truck is ugly') treated as a serious confession, and Dennis's disproportionate 'I call bullshit on that' treating it as a factual dispute, is a solid bit.

jokes.text: Frank: 'It's time we connect the Legos here and boil down to our core values. Hammer down on our brand identity and come out open commando.'
jokes.setup: Frank takes control of the meeting
jokes.punchline: 'Connect the Legos' and 'open commando' are Frank's versions of corporate buzzwords — close to real phrases ('connect the dots,' 'open kimono') but subtly wrong
jokes.explanation: 'Connect the Legos' instead of 'connect the dots' and 'open commando' instead of 'open kimono' — Frank's near-miss corporate buzzwords reveal he's absorbed the cadence but mangled the vocabulary. 'Come out open commando' has a funny double meaning (going commando = no underwear) that makes Frank's phrase inadvertently raunchier.

jokes.text: Dee: 'I said the commando thing.' Dennis: 'Didn't make sense the first time.' Dee: 'I thought it was cool and I want to circle back.' Dennis: 'If you're doing it because it's cool...'
jokes.setup: Frank uses 'open commando,' which Dee first used earlier
jokes.punchline: Dee defends her term not because it's accurate but because it 'sounded cool,' and Dennis's 'didn't make sense the first time' is doubly deflating
jokes.explanation: Decent callback. Dennis's 'didn't make sense the first time' as meta-commentary on Dee's earlier buzzword is a good structure, though the callback target wasn't strong enough to make this land big.

jokes.text: "No comment. That said, we are no longer gonna drink, serve, or have anything to do that represents water. Water is not the cornerstone of our company. And we will hereby be getting rid of the watercooler."
jokes.setup: The gang finally delivers their statement to the reporter after all the deliberation
jokes.punchline: Their official statement is: (1) no comment, and (2) they're banning water from their bar — a non-sequitur designed to destroy the evidence of their corporate awakening
jokes.explanation: The statement that solves the crisis by eliminating the watercooler — the source of all the trouble — is a good full-circle joke. 'Water is not the cornerstone of our company' is a memorably absurd business statement. Well-structured payoff to the watercooler framing device.

jokes.text: The gang finally delivers their statement to the reporter: 'No comment.'
jokes.setup: The entire episode has been an elaborate internal meeting to craft a statement for the press
jokes.punchline: After all the corporate-speak, strategy meetings, blame-shifting, and planning, the final statement is 'No comment'
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the entire episode's premise: all that effort, all that corporate-speak, all that blame-shifting — and the answer was always 'no comment.' The economy is flawless (maximum payoff per word). What elevates it is the CONTINUATION — Dennis then immediately starts explaining the watercooler, completely undermining the 'no comment' with unprompted confession. Classic Sunny: they can't even execute the simplest solution.

jokes.text: Following 'No comment,' Dennis immediately elaborates: 'That said, we are no longer gonna drink, serve, or have anything to do that represents water... we will hereby be getting rid of the watercooler.' Waitress: 'I'm not sure what you're talking about.'
jokes.setup: Dennis announces 'no comment' as the official statement
jokes.punchline: He then immediately volunteers that they're banning water and getting rid of the watercooler — essentially confessing to the existence of the scheme
jokes.explanation: Dennis can't help himself — 'no comment' immediately becomes a press release about their guilt. The 'we over-hydrated' explanation as the root of everything is a funny pseudo-mea-culpa that explains nothing while confessing everything.

jokes.text: "Sorry. We got on talking like this when we started over-hydrating."
jokes.setup: The reporter is confused by their corporate-speak statement about water
jokes.punchline: Mac explains their corporate vocabulary was caused by over-hydration — the entire episode's jargon is attributed to drinking too much water
jokes.explanation: Great retroactive joke — the entire corporate vocabulary was 'over-hydration' speaking. It's both a funny explanation and a good structural closing of the episode's central premise. 'Over-hydrating' as a pejorative is funny.

jokes.text: The 'reporter' says 'I'm sorry, do you think I'm a reporter? No. I'm here for the orgy.'
jokes.setup: The entire episode has been structured around managing a reporter who could expose them
jokes.punchline: She's not a reporter — she's a client for Frank's basement orgy
jokes.explanation: The episode's big structural twist: the entire premise — crafting a statement for the reporter — was built on a false assumption. Everything they did was unnecessary. This is a structurally excellent episode-closing reveal that reframes all the preceding corporate-speak as even more absurd. Great economy, strong structural payoff, and the reveal lands with appropriate weight.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Oh. Hey, guys, the whore is here.' Then argument about whether eleven men + one woman is an orgy or gangbang. 'That's a gangbang, yeah.'
jokes.setup: Frank's client arrives and is presented to the group
jokes.punchline: Frank greets her as 'the whore,' then the gang gets into a semantic debate about whether the situation constitutes an orgy or gangbang
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'the whore is here' is said with the same energy as 'the pizza is here.' The orgy vs. gangbang semantic debate is funny because it's the gang applying their characteristic over-analysis to something they should probably not be analyzing at all, with 'that's a gangbang, yeah' as a matter-of-fact conclusion.

jokes.text: "I told you guys, man. That's one woman. Yeah. T-That's not an orgy. That's a... No. No. That's a gangbang. No. No."
jokes.setup: Frank announces 'the orgy' has arrived — it's one woman
jokes.punchline: Charlie points out one woman does not constitute an orgy; someone (or multiple someones) escalate to the specific correct term; this is rejected with horror
jokes.explanation: The taxonomic correction — 'that's not an orgy, that's a gangbang' — with the chorus of 'No. No.' rejecting the accurate term is very funny. The gang is comfortable with the idea of an orgy but the accurate word horrifies them. Good escalation.

jokes.text: 'We really should find a way to exit Frank.'
jokes.setup: Frank is revealed to be running an ongoing basement orgy operation and has just greeted a sex worker
jokes.punchline: Dennis's response to all of this is the HR-speak 'exit Frank' — firing him from the group using corporate language
jokes.explanation: 'Exit Frank' as the final line of the episode uses HR euphemism ('exit' = fire/remove) for what is essentially expelling a family member from existence. Perfect economy — two words that close the episode's corporate-speak theme while landing as a dark callback to the fall-person discussion. The episode ends on its thesis: they still can't stop talking like this.

tmdb_overview: Desperate to stave off a public relations nightmare, the Gang embraces their newfound corporate professionalism to strategically scapegoat one Paddy's employee to fall on the proverbial sword.
